scope: 58 uncertain items: the final slash pairs after the Phase 1 cleanup (2026-11-05)

decision_procedure.cue_filter: single-word cues that are stopwords are dropped before scoring (calibration finding: they fire everywhere)
decision_procedure.abstain: otherwise render the slash form and log 'context did not settle it'
decision_procedure.logging: record chosen candidate, cue(s) that fired, scores for all candidates
decision_procedure.topic_cap: topic cues score +1 each, capped at +2 per candidate

logging: For every decided case record: heard form, chosen candidate, cues that fired, all candidate scores, method (adjacent/rules/embed/hybrid/llm). Abstentions render the slash form.

items.slot_note: Trap. 'gives' is normally a verb; the technical candidate is a noun phrase. ASR produced 'gives' for spoken 'Gibbs' (attested, Stan). Decisive pattern: 'gives free energy' as a noun-phrase slot occurs where a verb is missing or where the following words are 'free energy' plus a verb (is/equals/reduces). Ordinary 'gives' is followed by an object noun phrase and preceded by a subject noun/pronoun.

candidates.label: Gibbs free energy
negative_cues: gives a value of the (ordinary ditransitive)
candidates.notes: Attested mishearing (Stan). Source usage: 'Gibbs free energy (G) ... defined as G = H - TS'; 'free energy change may be expressed as delta G = delta H - T delta S'.

candidates.label: gives (ordinary verb)
candidates.notes: Structural: subject + gives + object is the default English verb pattern; choose ordinary when a grammatical subject and object bracket the word.

items.slot_note: Trap, same family as 'gives'. 'ideas' is normally a plural noun; the technical candidate is the noun phrase 'Gibbs free energy'. Decisive pattern is the same as for 'gives': the slot is followed by 'free energy' plus a verb (is/equals/change), leaving no verb for an ordinary 'ideas' reading, or the topic is spontaneity/equilibrium. Ordinary 'ideas' is bracketed by verbs or determiners and followed by ordinary nouns or relative clauses. Phonetically weaker than gives/Gibbs, so strength is medium, not strong.

candidates.label: Gibbs free energy
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Gibbs free energy (G) ... defined as G = H - TS'; 'free energy change is a reliable indicator of the spontaneity of a process'. Phonetic distance ideas/Gibbs is larger than gives/Gibbs, hence medium.

candidates.label: ideas (ordinary plural noun)
candidates.notes: Structural: plural count noun after determiner/adjective and before a verb or preposition is the default reading; choose ordinary unless 'free energy' immediately follows.

items.slot_note: Not true slot alternatives in running text: 'virial coefficient' is a noun phrase naming a constant (B, C); 'virial equation' names the series/equation of state. The word AFTER the slot usually decides: 'coefficient' following means the speaker continued the noun phrase; an 'equation' slot appears where a verb such as 'gives/writes/use' precedes or 'of state' follows.

candidates.label: virial equation
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'virial equation of state ... polynomial in density'; coefficients B2, B3 are fit to data.

candidates.label: virial coefficient
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'B2 is called the second virial coefficient'; 'coefficients are typically fit to experimental data and are temperature dependent'.

candidates.label: viral (ordinary)
candidates.notes: Structural: ordinary adjective for virus-related or rapidly spreading content; no ChemE source needed and none claimed.

items.slot_note: Part-of-speech alternatives: 'azeotrope' is a noun (a mixture); 'azeotropic' is an adjective and must be followed by a noun (mixture, distillation, composition, behaviour). The following word decides: a noun after the slot -> azeotropic; a verb or determiner pattern ('an azeotrope forms/is') -> azeotrope.

candidates.label: azeotrope
phrase_patterns: the azeotrope has a characteristic boiling point
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'An azeotrope is a mixture that exhibits the same concentration in the vapor phase and the liquid phase'; 'Each azeotrope has a characteristic boiling point'.

candidates.label: azeotropic
negative_cues: is a mixture (noun-phrase predicate after slot)
candidates.notes: Structural adjective slot, supported by source collocations 'azeotropic distillation is usually used' (Wikipedia) and 'azeotropic mixture' in dictionary usage derived from the same article family; adjective-before-noun is the decisive structural cue.

items.slot_note: Same candidate set as azee-o-trope (identical spoken target, different ASR spelling of the heard form). Coordinator-authored at merge by cloning the azee-o-trope item; cues and sources carry over unchanged.

candidates.label: azeotrope
phrase_patterns: the azeotrope has a characteristic boiling point
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'An azeotrope is a mixture that exhibits the same concentration in the vapor phase and the liquid phase'; 'Each azeotrope has a characteristic boiling point'.

candidates.label: azeotropic
negative_cues: is a mixture (noun-phrase predicate after slot)
candidates.notes: Structural adjective slot, supported by source collocations 'azeotropic distillation is usually used' (Wikipedia) and 'azeotropic mixture' in dictionary usage derived from the same article family; adjective-before-noun is the decisive structural cue.

items.slot_note: Two-word slot. Technical 'dew point' is a noun: a temperature at which vapour condenses / air reaches saturation. It appears after 'the', 'at the', 'reach the', 'below the' and before 'temperature', 'is', 'of the air'. Ordinary 'do point' is not an idiom; an ordinary reading needs 'do' as a verb ('do point out', 'do point to') or a list instruction ('do point 2'). The following word decides: 'point out/to' after the slot rules the technical reading out; 'temperature/is' after it rules the ordinary reading out.

candidates.label: dew point
phrase_patterns: temperature at which air reaches saturation
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Dew Point is the temperature at which air reaches 100 percent relative humidity. If the air is cooled below dew point, moisture in the air condenses'; 'At the dew point temperature, relative humidity is 100%'.

candidates.label: do point (ordinary verb + noun/verb)
candidates.notes: Structural: 'do' as emphatic/main verb requires a following base verb or object; 'point out/to' directly after the slot is decisive for ordinary. Weak as a standalone collocation because 'do point' alone is not idiomatic English.

items.slot_note: Alternatives share the head word Carnot and differ in the following noun: cycle, engine or efficiency. The word AFTER the slot is the decisive cue; do not decide from the head word alone.

candidates.label: Carnot cycle
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'He devised a theoretical cycle, now called the Carnot cycle'; 'The cycle comprises two isothermal and two adiabatic processes'.

candidates.label: Carnot engine
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Any heat engine employing the Carnot cycle is called a Carnot engine'; 'A Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures has the greatest possible efficiency'.

candidates.label: Carnot efficiency
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the maximum or Carnot efficiency is given by Eff = 1 - Tc/Th', with reservoir temperatures in kelvins.

items.slot_note: Trap + alternatives sharing a head noun slot: 'Carnot cycle', 'Carnot engine' and 'Carnot efficiency' are variants decided almost entirely by the word AFTER the slot (cycle/engine/efficiency) or by a preceding 'the ...' with heat-engine topic words. Ordinary 'cannot' is a modal verb: the next word is a base verb (be, exceed, do, separate).

candidates.label: Carnot cycle
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The cycle comprises two isothermal and two adiabatic processes'; 'He devised a theoretical cycle, now called the Carnot cycle'.

candidates.label: Carnot engine
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Any heat engine employing the Carnot cycle is called a Carnot engine'; 'A Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures has the greatest possible efficiency'.

candidates.label: Carnot efficiency
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the maximum or Carnot efficiency is given by Eff = 1 - Tc/Th'.

candidates.label: cannot (ordinary modal)
candidates.notes: Structural: modal + base verb is decisive; a following noun (cycle/engine/efficiency) rules the modal reading out grammatically.

items.slot_note: Part-of-speech alternatives. Technical 'laminar' is an adjective and must be followed by a noun, almost always 'flow', or by 'or turbulent'. Ordinary 'laminate' is a noun (a layered material, a flooring, an ID card) or a verb (to laminate). The word after the slot decides: 'flow/regime/boundary layer' -> laminar; 'flooring/surface/paper/it' -> laminate.

candidates.label: laminar
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'For NR below about 2000, flow is laminar'; 'flow in a very smooth tube will be laminar at low velocity'; glossary 'laminar: smooth and regular, flowing as though in different layers'.

candidates.label: laminate (ordinary material/verb)
candidates.notes: Structural: noun after determiner with material adjectives, or verb with a direct object; an adjective slot before 'flow' cannot be filled by 'laminate'.

items.slot_note: Weak pair: 'Hagen-Poiseuille' and 'Poiseuille's law' name the same law/equation in the sources, so most context fits both. Only two cues separate them: a preceding 'Hagen' (or a following 'equation/flow') points to the compound name, and a following 'law' or 'states/says' points to Poiseuille's law. Otherwise abstain.

candidates.label: Hagen–Poiseuille
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, also known as the Hagen-Poiseuille law, Poiseuille law or Poiseuille equation, is a physical law that gives the pressure drop in an incompressible and Newtonian fluid in laminar flow'. The source treats the names as synonyms, hence only moderate.

candidates.label: Poiseuille's law
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Poiseuille's law is the physical law concerning the voluminal laminar stationary flow of an incompressible uniform viscous liquid through a cylindrical tube'; the same source notes it is 'also sometimes called the Hagen-Poiseuille law'.

items.slot_note: Alternatives share the head word Moody and differ in the following noun: chart or diagram, which the sources use as synonyms for the same plot. The word AFTER the slot is the only technical cue. Ordinary 'moody' is an adjective for a person.

candidates.label: Moody chart
phrase_patterns: read the friction factor from the Moody chart
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the Moody chart or Moody diagram (also Stanton diagram) is a graph... that relates the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor, Reynolds number Re, and surface roughness'.

candidates.label: Moody diagram
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'In 1944, Lewis Ferry Moody plotted the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor against Reynolds number Re for various values of relative roughness. This chart became commonly known as the Moody chart or Moody diagram'.

candidates.label: moody (ordinary)
candidates.notes: Structural: ordinary adjective for a person in low or changeable spirits; a following noun chart/diagram rules it out grammatically in this slot.

items.slot_note: Trap. Technical 'Mach number' is a dimensionless ratio (flow velocity / speed of sound); the word after the slot is normally 'number', or a numeral/value, or 'one' in 'Mach one'. Ordinary 'mock' is an adjective (mock exam/test/trial) or a verb (to mock). 'Number' or a flow-regime word (subsonic, supersonic) after the slot decides for Mach; 'exam/test/interview' after it decides for ordinary.

candidates.label: Mach number
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the Mach number is defined as the ratio of the current speed to the speed of sound'; flows are called subsonic, supersonic, sonic, transonic, hypersonic by Mach number range.

candidates.label: mock (ordinary adjective/verb)
candidates.notes: Structural: adjective before assessment/imitation nouns, or verb with an object; neither can take 'number' as the following noun in the dimensionless-ratio sense.

items.slot_note: Trap. Technical 'Froude number' is a dimensionless ratio (inertia force / gravity force) for free-surface and open-channel flow; the word after the slot is 'number', or the slot stands before 'is less than 1 / greater than 1' with subcritical/supercritical nearby. Ordinary 'fraud' is a noun for deception, bracketed by articles and legal verbs. 'Number' after the slot is decisive for Froude.

candidates.label: Froude number
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the Froude number is the ratio of inertia force to gravity force'; 'When the Froude number is 1, the velocity is equal to the velocity of wave propagation'; approach-flow Froude number 'less than 0.5' for measurement.

candidates.label: fraud (ordinary noun)
candidates.notes: Structural: deception noun with legal/financial modifiers and verbs (commit, detect, charge); a following 'number' rules this reading out.

items.slot_note: Alternatives share the head word Euler and differ in the following noun: number or equation. The word AFTER the slot is the decisive cue. A third reading, ordinary 'oiler', is a person or device that oils machinery, or an oil tanker.

candidates.label: Euler number
phrase_patterns: the Euler number is defined as
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The Euler number (Eu) is a dimensionless number used in fluid flow calculations. It expresses the relationship between a local pressure drop... and the kinetic energy per volume'.

candidates.label: Euler equation
phrase_patterns: the Euler equations govern inviscid flow
topic_cues: conservation of mass momentum and energy
candidates.notes: Source usage (plural in the source): 'the Euler equations are a set of partial differential equations governing adiabatic and inviscid flow... correspond to the Navier-Stokes equations with zero viscosity'.

candidates.label: oiler (ordinary)
candidates.notes: Structural: ordinary noun for a device/person that applies oil, or a tanker ship; no ChemE source needed and none claimed.

items.slot_note: Same pair as 'oiler', heard here in a form closer to the name itself. Alternatives share the head word Euler and differ in the following noun: number or equation. The word AFTER the slot is the decisive cue.

candidates.label: Euler number
phrase_patterns: the Euler number is defined as
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The Euler number (Eu) is a dimensionless number... relationship between a local pressure drop... and the kinetic energy per volume of the flow'.

candidates.label: Euler equation
phrase_patterns: the Euler equations govern inviscid flow
topic_cues: conservation of mass momentum and energy
candidates.notes: Source usage (plural in the source): 'the Euler equations are a set of partial differential equations governing adiabatic and inviscid flow'.

items.slot_note: Opposite rheology classes: pseudoplastic is shear-thinning and dilatant is shear-thickening. The direction of the viscosity change with shear rate, stated on either side of the slot, is decisive; the fluid name alone is not.

candidates.label: pseudoplastic
phrase_patterns: viscosity decreases with increasing shear rate
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Shear-thinning (pseudoplastic): Viscosity decreases as shear rate increases'; 'Pseudoplastic fluids such as paint and ketchup exhibit shear thinning'.

candidates.label: dilatant
phrase_patterns: viscosity increases with increasing shear rate
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Shear-thickening (dilatant): Viscosity increases with rising shear rate'; 'Dilatant fluids exhibit shear thickening properties... A mixture of cornstarch and water'.

items.slot_note: Trap. Technical 'Rayleigh number' is a dimensionless group for buoyancy-driven (natural/free) convection, Ra = Gr x Pr; the word after the slot is 'number', often with 'critical' before it or a large power-of-ten value after it. Ordinary 'rally' is a noun (a gathering, a market recovery) or a verb (to rally). 'Number' after the slot is decisive for Rayleigh.

candidates.label: Rayleigh number
phrase_patterns: Rayleigh number is the product of Grashof and Prandtl
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Rayleigh number (Ra) ... dimensionless number associated with buoyancy-driven flow, also known as free (or natural) convection'; 'defined as the product of the Grashof number (Gr) and the Prandtl number (Pr)'; below a critical value 'heat transfer is purely by conduction'.

candidates.label: rally (ordinary noun/verb)
candidates.notes: Structural: gathering/recovery noun with place or supporter phrases, or verb with around/behind/against; a following 'number' rules this reading out.

items.slot_note: Same-word alternatives plus an adjective form. Technical 'fin' (heat transfer) is an extended surface: it takes 'efficiency', 'effectiveness', 'tip', 'base', 'length' nearby and verbs such as 'attach/add'. 'finned' is the adjective form and must precede a noun (surface, tube, exchanger). Ordinary 'fin' is the fish/shark appendage, or a verb in finance slang is not in play here. Topic decides when grammar does not: radiator/heat sink/exchanger versus shark/dorsal.

candidates.label: fin (heat-transfer extended surface)
candidates.notes: Source usage (ChemE lecture): 'increase in surface area by attaching extended surfaces called fins'; 'Fin efficiency ... actual heat transfer rate from the fin / ideal ... if the entire fin were at base temperature'; examples 'thin rods on condenser', 'car radiator'.

candidates.label: finned
phrase_patterns: finned surfaces are commonly used to enhance heat transfer
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Finned surfaces are commonly used in practice to enhance heat transfer'; adjective slot directly before surface/tube/exchanger is decisive.

candidates.label: fin (ordinary animal appendage)
candidates.notes: Structural/ordinary usage: animal anatomy noun with dorsal/pectoral modifiers; no heat-transfer source claimed.

items.slot_note: Trap in the opposite direction to 'fin': here the heard word is the ordinary adjective 'thin', and the technical candidates are 'fin' (noun) and 'finned' (adjective). A technical reading requires the slot to sit where 'thin' is ungrammatical: before 'efficiency/effectiveness' (fin) or where a following noun is surface/tube and 'thin' would need a second adjective. In most running text 'thin film/layer/shell/wall' is correct as heard and must not be changed; strength for the technical candidates is therefore weak-to-medium and topic-gated.

candidates.label: fin (heat-transfer extended surface)
candidates.notes: Source usage as for 'fin' item. Weak here because the collocation must override a grammatical, very common adjective reading of the heard word; require 'efficiency/effectiveness' directly after the slot plus extended-surface topic words.

candidates.label: finned
negative_cues: thin film (established technical phrase as heard)
candidates.notes: Mis-targeting risk is high: 'thin film' is itself a standard phrase (thin-film boiling/evaporation), so a following 'film' is a strong negative cue, not support. Use only when 'thin' + surface/tube is ungrammatical in context and fin topic words are present.

candidates.label: thin (ordinary adjective, as heard)
candidates.notes: Structural: adjective directly before a noun is the default reading and several of those phrases (thin film, thin shell) are themselves technical; do not replace without the fin-specific right cues.

items.slot_note: Trap. Technical candidate is 'nucleate boiling' — spoken 'nucleate' (noo-klee-ayt) misheard as 'nuclear'. The slot is followed by 'boiling' and sits on the boiling curve: bubbles forming at nucleation sites, before transition/film boiling, up to the critical heat flux. Ordinary 'nuclear' is followed by power/energy/weapons/reactor/family and never by 'boiling' in its ordinary sense. 'Boiling' directly after the slot plus boiling-curve topic words is decisive.

candidates.label: nucleate boiling
phrase_patterns: transition from natural convection to nucleate boiling
candidates.notes: Source usage (NPTEL boiling lecture): 'Nucleate Boiling: it commences with the increased difference... bubbles grow, separate from the heated surface'; 'transition from natural convection to nucleate boiling'; 'correlations in pool boiling: nucleate saturated pool boiling'.

candidates.label: nuclear (ordinary adjective)
candidates.notes: Structural: adjective before energy/power/reactor nouns; a following 'boiling' rules this reading out in a heat-transfer talk.

items.slot_note: Flow-arrangement pair for two streams (usually in a heat exchanger or contactor). The heard form is ambiguous between the two spoken words; the arrangement described around the slot decides: same direction/same end is cocurrent, opposite directions/opposite ends is countercurrent.

candidates.label: countercurrent
phrase_patterns: fluids enter at opposite ends and flow in opposite directions
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'In countercurrent flow, the two flows move in opposite directions'; for exchangers, 'the LMTD of a countercurrent flow arrangement shows to be much higher than in a cocurrent arrangement'.

candidates.label: cocurrent
phrase_patterns: fluids flow in the same direction
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'In the cocurrent flow exchange mechanism, the two fluids flow in the same direction'; 'one set up is where the fluids are both flowing in the same direction (co-current)'.

items.slot_note: Trap. Technical use is a two-name method: spoken 'Rachford rice' surfaces in ASR as e.g. 'ratchford rice' or a lone 'rice' when the first name is garbled. Local cues are flash/VLE words on either side; ordinary 'rice' is food/agriculture with cooking verbs and measures.

candidates.label: Rachford–Rice
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the value of V can be calculated by the solution of the non-linear Rachford-Rice equation'; 'flash calculations are applied for processes involving vapour/liquid equilibrium (VLE)'.

candidates.label: rice (ordinary food)
candidates.notes: Structural/ordinary usage: food noun with cooking and quantity collocations; no technical source claimed.

items.slot_note: Three roles in liquid-liquid extraction, not three names for one thing. The role described around the slot decides: the liquid added to extract is the solvent, the component transferred/recovered is the solute, and the original carrier liquid in the feed is the diluent.

candidates.label: solvent
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'solvent is the immiscible liquid we add to create a new liquid phase'; 'the solute-rich solvent is called the extract'.

candidates.label: solute
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Solute is the component that we are interested in extracting'; 'allowing the solute to transfer from the feed to the solvent'.

candidates.label: diluent
phrase_patterns: the diluent is the liquid in the original solution
diluent is the carrier of solute in the feed stream
raffinate, consisting of the solute and the diluent
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'diluent is the carrier of solute in the feed stream'; 'The diluent is the liquid in the original solution other than the solute', from the extraction text reproduced in the search result.

items.slot_note: Two features of the same ternary/tie-line diagram talk. A tie line is a line (it connects, slopes, has endpoints); a plait point is a point (curves meet there, tie lines shrink to it, the two phase compositions become identical there). The noun/verb pattern around the slot decides.

candidates.label: tie line
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the tie lines are straight lines that connect the compositions of the vapor and liquid phase in equilibrium'; 'any mixture on a tie line has the same liquid and vapor compositions'.

candidates.label: plait point
phrase_patterns: the plait point is the point at which
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the bubble point curve and the dew point curve, both of which meet at the plait point. This is the point at which the liquid and vapor composition are identical'.

items.slot_note: Two outlet streams of a membrane unit. What the stream does at the membrane decides: passes through is permeate; does not pass / is retained, concentrated or recycled is retentate. The heard form favours retentate, but a 'passes through' clause overrides it.

candidates.label: permeate
phrase_patterns: the permeate passes through the membrane
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The portion of the suspension that passes through the membrane is called the permeate while the portion that does not is called the retentate'; 'permeate is collected'.

candidates.label: retentate
phrase_patterns: the retentate is returned to the tank
negative_cues: passes through the membrane (as the stream's own action)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The retentate is returned to the tank holding the solution'; 'the retentate, sometimes called the concentrate, is the liquid that is blocked and remains on the upstream side of the membrane'.

items.slot_note: Singular/plural pair for the same dimensionless group (symbol Da, defined as a ratio of reaction rate to transport rate). 'number' (singular) is the generic definition slot; 'numbers' (plural) appears when more than one is in play, typically the first and second, DaI and DaII. Verb agreement and a preceding 'two/these/first and second' decide.

candidates.label: Damköhler number
negative_cues: first and second (as the slot's own frame)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The Damköhler number (Da) is defined as the dimensionless ratio of the reaction rate to the rate of mass transfer'; 'The Damköhler numbers (Da) are dimensionless numbers that relate the chemical reaction timescale to the transport phenomena rate'.

candidates.label: Damköhler numbers
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the first Damköhler number (DaI) considers the relative rates of reaction and convective transport, whereas the second Damköhler number (DaII) considers the relative rates of reaction and diffusion'. Plural talk is less frequent than the singular definition, hence moderate.

items.slot_note: Same singular/plural pair as 'dam-kurler', heard here as two words. 'number' (singular) is the generic definition slot; 'numbers' (plural) appears when the first and second numbers, DaI and DaII, are both in play. Verb agreement and a preceding 'two/these/first and second' decide.

candidates.label: Damköhler number
negative_cues: first and second (as the slot's own frame)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'The Damköhler number (Da) is defined as the dimensionless ratio of the reaction rate to the rate of mass transfer, indicating whether a reaction is limited by reaction kinetics or mass transport'.

candidates.label: Damköhler numbers
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the first Damköhler number (DaI) considers the relative rates of reaction and convective transport, whereas the second Damköhler number (DaII) considers the relative rates of reaction and diffusion'.

items.slot_note: Review-list item, approved as a slash pair waiving the length limit. All four technical candidates are ways a catalyst loses activity; 'deactivation' is the umbrella noun and the other three are its named mechanisms, so a mechanism word nearby (sulfur, coke, high temperature) selects the mechanism, while a bare 'loss of activity over time' selects deactivation. Only 'sintering' is phonetically close to the heard form; the other three rely on topic cues alone and are weak. Ordinary 'centering' is positioning something at a centre.

candidates.label: poisoning
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Poisoning: impurities in the feed (e.g., sulfur compounds) bind irreversibly to active sites, blocking them'; 'Poisons, such as sulfur compounds, stick permanently to the active sites'. Weak: phonetically distant from 'centering'; topic cues only.

candidates.label: deactivation
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'catalysts lose their effectiveness through several deactivation mechanisms' followed by the poisoning/fouling/sintering list; 'Main mechanisms: poisoning, coking/fouling, sintering'. Weak: as the umbrella term it overlaps every mechanism cue.

candidates.label: fouling
negative_cues: sulfur binds to active sites (poisoning pattern)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Fouling: carbon deposits or other material physically coat the catalyst surface'; 'Coke covers sites and blocks pore mouths'. Weak: phonetically distant from 'centering'; topic cues only.

candidates.label: sintering
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Sintering: at high temperatures, small catalyst particles merge into larger ones, reducing the total surface area'; review list names sintering 'the phonetic near-spelling among the four', hence medium where the other three are weak.

candidates.label: centering (ordinary)
candidates.notes: Structural: gerund + object noun ('centering the text/image') is the default ordinary pattern; no technical source claimed.

items.slot_note: Overlapping instrument terms: sources note vendors use them interchangeably, so strength is moderate. The deciding context is the signal: a standardised 4-20 mA (or 1-5 V) signal sent to a controller over distance points to transmitter; conversion of one form of energy into another, or a millivolt/voltage output, points to transducer. The heard form favours transducer.

candidates.label: transmitter
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'a Transmitter is a device that transmits a standard instrumentation signal... The standard electrical signals are 1-5 V or 4-20 mA'; 'pressure transmitter has a low-impedance current output, most commonly designed to transmit analogue 4-20mA signals'.

candidates.label: transducer
phrase_patterns: transducer converts one form of energy into another
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'A transducer is a device that converts one form of energy to another... converts the reading into an electrical or electronic signal'; 'A transducer is a device that converts one form of energy into another form so it can be used for further processing'.

items.slot_note: Review-list item, approved as a slash pair waiving the length limit. Spoken 'pie' is the pi in the theorem name and in 'pi groups/terms'. The two technical candidates differ in scope: 'Buckingham Pi theorem' is the named result (n variables, m dimensions, n-m groups); 'dimensionless analysis' (source texts more often 'dimensional analysis') is the broader procedure around it. A 'theorem/groups = n minus m' pattern selects the theorem; a 'method/procedure/reduce the variables' pattern selects the analysis. Ordinary 'pie' is food.

candidates.label: dimensionless analysis
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'dimensional analysis, as this procedure is called'; 'Because any equation describing the world can be written in dimensionless form ... using dimensionless groups'. Label kept as in the review list ('dimensionless analysis'); sources use 'dimensional analysis' for the same procedure.

candidates.label: Buckingham Pi theorem
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'If there are n variables in a problem and these variables contain m primary dimensions ... the equation relating all the variables will have (n-m) dimensionless groups'; 'This shortcut, known as the Buckingham Pi theorem, is named after Edgar Buckingham and his uppercase Pi notation for dimensionless groups'.

candidates.label: pie (ordinary food)
candidates.notes: Structural: food/chart collocates are decisive ordinary patterns; no technical source claimed.

items.slot_note: Trap with a same-word technical phrase. 'Shell balance' is a method phrase: a momentum (or energy/mass) balance over a thin differential shell, used to derive a velocity profile. It appears with 'momentum balance', 'differential', 'set up/do a', and boundary-condition talk. Ordinary and other-technical 'shell' uses are far more frequent in ChemE speech: shell-and-tube exchanger, tube shell, seashell, shell company. Only the balance/momentum collocation supports the slash candidate; 'and tube' directly after the slot is a strong negative cue for it.

candidates.label: shell balance
phrase_patterns: rate of momentum in minus out (shell balance form)
a shell is a differential element
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'a shell balance can be used to determine the velocity profile'; '(Rate of momentum in) - (rate of momentum out) + (sum of all forces) = 0'; Clarkson notes: 'shell balances are useful devices for applying the principle of conservation of momentum... incompressible laminar flow in a straight circular pipe'.

candidates.label: shell (ordinary / other technical, as heard)
candidates.notes: Structural/ordinary usage: in ChemE speech 'shell and tube' and 'shell side' are the dominant collocations; keep the heard word unless 'balance' follows.

items.slot_note: MIS-TARGETED slash candidate — assessed against sources. A tray weir is itself the correct technical term: sources state liquid 'flows across a tray and then over a weir to enter into the downcomer' and 'the function of a weir is to maintain a desired liquid level on the tray', with 'weir height' and 'weir length' as design variables. 'Trays, downcomer' are neighbouring parts, not synonyms or expansions of 'weir', so replacing a correctly heard 'weir' with them loses the term and produces no grammatical phrase. The tray/downcomer cues below therefore support KEEPING 'weir', not the slash replacement; the slash candidate is scored weak and should normally abstain. A second, older technical sense of 'weir' (river/flow-measurement barrier, V-notch) is also correct as heard. Phase 1 adjudication (2026-11-05): the 'trays, downcomer' candidate is removed; the only candidate is 'weir' itself — the heard form is already the correct tray term, and the item remains in the rules set only because 'weir' is also an ordinary word, so the stage may confirm it from tray context or abstain to the weir/weir form.

candidates.label: weir
phrase_patterns: over the weir into the downcomer
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Liquid falls through the downcomers... A weir on the tray ensures that there is always some liquid (holdup) on the tray'; 'liquid flows across a tray and then over a weir to enter into the downcomer'; NPTEL tray design lists 'weir height, weir length, downcomer area' as separate layout quantities — proof weir is distinct from downcomer. (Merged with the duplicate 'weir' candidate at Phase 1: both readings keep the word as heard.)

items.slot_note: Trap plus the same mis-targeting as 'weir'. Ordinary 'we're' is the contraction we+are and is followed by a verb-ing, adjective, or noun phrase — the default in running speech. The plausible technical target when 'we're' is misheard in a tray talk is the single word 'weir' (tray outlet weir), not the slash phrase 'trays, downcomer', which cannot occupy this slot grammatically. Tray/downcomer topic words with an ungrammatical contraction reading (e.g. 'the liquid goes over we're into...') point to 'weir'; the 'trays, downcomer' candidate was removed at Phase 1; 'weir' is the only technical candidate.

candidates.label: weir
phrase_patterns: over the weir into the downcomer
candidates.notes: Source usage as for 'weir' item: liquid 'flows over a weir to enter into the downcomer'; weir height/length are tray design variables. Medium, not strong, because the contraction reading is usually correct and needs a broken grammar signal to override.

candidates.label: we're (ordinary contraction)
candidates.notes: Structural: we + are + verb-ing/adjective is the default spoken pattern and dominates transcripts; choose ordinary whenever the contraction reading is grammatical.

items.slot_note: Trap plus the same mis-targeting as 'weir'. Ordinary 'weird' is an adjective (strange) before nouns like result/behaviour/thing, or after 'is/looks'. The plausible technical target in a tray talk is 'weir' (one syllable, near-homophone), not the slash phrase 'trays, downcomer', which cannot fill an adjective slot. A tray/downcomer context where 'weird' is followed by height/length or 'into the downcomer' points to 'weir'; the 'trays, downcomer' candidate was removed at Phase 1; 'weir' is the only technical candidate.

candidates.label: weir
candidates.notes: Source usage as for 'weir' item. Medium because 'weird' as an adjective is grammatical in far more slots than the contraction case; require weir-specific right cues (height/length/downcomer).

candidates.label: weird (ordinary adjective)
candidates.notes: Structural: adjective in determiner+adjective+noun or copula+adjective slots is the default reading.

items.slot_note: Trap, case-sensitive in writing but not in speech. Technical 'FEED' is the all-caps acronym Front-End Engineering Design: a project phase, always in project-execution contexts (study, package, stage, cost estimate, EPC bid, final investment decision). In ChemE process speech the heard word 'feed' is overwhelmingly the process stream (feed rate, feed tray, feed composition) and must be kept. Only project-phase collocations support FEED; any stream/rate/tray/composition cue is a strong negative for it.

candidates.label: FEED (Front-End Engineering Design)
phrase_patterns: basis for bidding for EPC contracts
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) ... comes after the Conceptual design or Feasibility study'; 'The FEED package is used as the basis for bidding for Engineering, Procurement and Construction contracts (EPC)'; 'typically followed by Detailed Design'. Medium because speech carries no capitalisation; require explicit project-phase words.

candidates.label: feed (process stream, as heard)
candidates.notes: Structural/domain usage: 'feed' as the inlet stream noun with rate/stream/tray/composition modifiers is the standard ChemE collocation set; labelled ordinary here because it is the heard word used correctly, not the slash expansion.

items.slot_note: Trap and partly mis-targeted. 'Benzine' is itself a real substance name — petroleum benzine / petroleum ether, a mixture of light alkanes used as a nonpolar solvent — and sources warn explicitly that it 'should not be confused with benzene': benzene is the single cyclic aromatic compound C6H6. The slash candidate 'benzene' is justified only with aromatic/ring/C6H6/carcinogen collocations; solvent-mixture collocations (petroleum ether, naphtha, boiling range, alkanes) support keeping 'benzine'.

candidates.label: benzene
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Benzene (C6H6) is of great commercial importance... a known carcinogen, its use as an additive in gasoline is now limited'; contrast source: 'benzene is a cyclic, aromatic hydrocarbon' versus benzine as an alkane mixture.

candidates.label: benzine (petroleum benzine, as heard)
phrase_patterns: benzine is a mixture of alkanes
petroleum ether, also known as benzine

(Benzine is a mixture of alkanes, such as pentane, hexane, and heptane...)'; 'Petroleum benzine is a hydrocarbon-based solvent mixture... classified by its physical properties (e.g. boiling point)'. Labelled ordinary as the heard word used correctly.

items.slot_note: Trap and often mis-targeted in the reverse direction. 'Ammonium' (NH4+, the ion) and 'ammonia' (NH3, the neutral molecule/gas) differ by one proton and are both correct technical words; sources stress students 'commonly confuse ammonia with ammonium'. The slash candidate 'ammonia' is justified only with NH3/gas/synthesis collocations (ammonia synthesis, Haber, anhydrous, refrigeration, accepts a proton). Salt and ion collocations — ammonium chloride/sulfate/nitrate, ammonium ion, NH4+ — support keeping 'ammonium' and are strong negative cues for the slash candidate.

candidates.label: ammonia
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Ammonia and water molecules are reactants, while the ammonium ion and the hydroxide ion are products: NH3 + H2O -> NH4+ + OH-'; 'ammonia acts as a base... a proton acceptor'. Medium because the heard word is itself usually correct.

candidates.label: ammonium (ion/salts, as heard)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the ammonium ion, NH4+, donates a proton'; 'ammonia reacts with water to produce the ammonium cation'; 'species ammonia and ammonium differ by only a hydrogen ion... a conjugate pair'. Labelled ordinary as the heard word used correctly.

items.slot_note: Narrowing, not a synonym: 'ketone' is a class (carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons); 'methyl ethyl ketone' (MEK, butanone) is one member. The specific candidate is justified only when the talk names MEK's own collocations — solvent use with resins/coatings, butanone, MEK, acetone comparison. Generic ketone talk (acetone, cyclohexanone, class properties, naming) keeps 'ketone'. LibreTexts lists 'acetone, methylethyl ketone, and cyclohexanone' as the most important ketones, so an unqualified slot is genuinely ambiguous; strength medium.

candidates.label: methyl ethyl ketone
phrase_patterns: butanone, also known as methyl ethyl ketone
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Butanone, also known as methyl ethyl ketone (MEK)... commonly used as an industrial solvent... used in processes involving gums, resins, cellulose acetate and nitrocellulose coatings'; LibreTexts: 'the most important ketones are acetone, methylethyl ketone, and cyclohexanone'.

candidates.label: ketone (class name, as heard)
phrase_patterns: the carbonyl carbon of a ketone
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'In a ketone, the carbon atom of a carbonyl is bonded to two other carbons'; common names are 'substituent groups listed alphabetically + ketone'. Labelled ordinary as the heard word used correctly (class-level talk).

items.slot_note: MIS-TARGETED slash candidate. An aldehyde and methyl ethyl ketone are different functional classes: sources define an aldehyde by a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydrogen, a ketone by a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons, and MEK (butanone) is explicitly a ketone — 'this colorless liquid ketone'. No collocation makes 'aldehyde' a mishearing of 'methyl ethyl ketone' (no phonetic or semantic path). The slash candidate is scored weak with no supporting phrase patterns; the correct action in aldehyde contexts is to keep 'aldehyde' (or a named aldehyde such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde). Phase 1 fix 8 (2026-11-05): the methyl ethyl ketone candidate is removed; the only candidate is 'aldehyde' itself, so the stage may confirm the word as heard from aldehyde-class context or abstain to the aldehyde/aldehyde form.

candidates.label: aldehyde
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Carbonyl groups define two related families: the aldehydes and the ketones... In an aldehyde, at least one of the attached groups must be a hydrogen atom'; examples formaldehyde, benzaldehyde (flavouring). Labelled ordinary as the heard word used correctly.

items.slot_note: Adjective pair: both must be followed by a noun (mixture, catalyst, catalysis, reaction, phase). The phase relation described around the slot decides: same phase/uniform throughout is homogeneous; different phases/non-uniform is heterogeneous.

candidates.label: homogeneous
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'If its composition is uniform throughout, it is a homogeneous mixture'; 'In a homogeneous reaction, the catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants'.

candidates.label: heterogeneous
phrase_patterns: on the surface of the catalyst
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'a heterogeneous mixture is distinguished by the fact that different samples of the mixture may have a different composition'; 'In a heterogeneous reaction, the catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants... a solid catalyst with the reactants as either liquids or gases'.

items.slot_note: Pair from one equation, A v = lambda v: the eigenvalue is the scalar (lambda, found from the characteristic polynomial/determinant), the eigenvector is the non-zero vector (direction unchanged, found by solving). Words for scalar/values/roots point one way; words for vector/direction/solution point the other.

candidates.label: eigenvalue
negative_cues: vector (as the slot's own following noun)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'An eigenvalue of A is a scalar lambda such that the equation Av = lambda v has a nontrivial solution'; 'Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are only for square matrices'.

candidates.label: eigenvector
negative_cues: values of the matrix (as the slot's frame)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'An eigenvector of A is a nonzero vector v in R^n such that Av = lambda v, for some scalar lambda'; 'Av and v lie on the same line through the origin'.

items.slot_note: Activity versus instrument: 'surveying' is the field/activity (a gerund: in/for surveying, land surveying) and cannot take an article or a plural; 'theodolite' is a countable instrument noun (a/the theodolite, set up, telescope, measures angles). Article or instrument verbs around the slot decide.

candidates.label: surveying
negative_cues: a the (article directly before the slot, instrument slot)
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'Surveying or land surveying is the technique, profession, art, and science of determining the terrestrial positions of points based on the distances and angles between them... used to establish maps and boundaries'.

candidates.label: theodolite
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'A theodolite is a precision optical instrument for measuring angles between designated visible points in the horizontal and vertical planes. The traditional use has been for land surveying'; 'It consists of a movable telescope'.

items.slot_note: Trap, cross-domain. Technical 'phasor' is a complex number representing a sinusoid (amplitude and phase) for AC steady-state analysis; its collocations are phasor diagram/domain/representation, impedance, voltage/current phasors, RLC circuits. Ordinary 'phaser' is a fictional weapon or an audio phase-shifting effect. Note the phasor article itself carries 'Not to be confused with phaser'. In ChemE speech phasor arises only in instrumentation/AC-circuit asides, so require electrical collocations; strength medium.

candidates.label: phasor
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'a phasor... is a complex number representing a sinusoidal function whose amplitude and initial phase are time-invariant'; 'phasor transform allows the analysis of the AC steady state of RLC circuits'; the complex constant 'is known as a phasor, or complex amplitude'.

candidates.label: phaser (ordinary fiction/audio)
candidates.notes: Structural/ordinary usage: fiction weapon with 'set to stun', or audio effect with pedal/effect/sweep collocations; no technical source claimed.

items.slot_note: Trap, cross-domain and rare in ChemE speech. Technical 'balun' (balanced-to-unbalanced) is an electrical device interfacing balanced and unbalanced transmission lines, at antenna feed points, coax to twin-lead/dipole. Ordinary 'balloon' is the inflatable object (also weather balloon, balloon payment, to balloon = swell). Only antenna/coax/balanced-line collocations support balun; strength weak-to-medium because the base rate in chemical-engineering lectures is very low.

right_cues: between the cable and the antenna
phrase_patterns: balun at the antenna feed point
balun between the cable and the antenna feed
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'a balun (from balanced to unbalanced) is an electrical device that allows balanced and unbalanced lines to be interfaced'; 'baluns are typically used as a form of common mode choke attached at the antenna feed point'; conversion of '300-ohm twin-lead (balanced) to 75-ohm coaxial cable (unbalanced)'. candidates.label: balloon (ordinary noun/verb)
candidates.notes: Structural/ordinary usage: inflatable noun with inflate/helium/rise collocations, or finance/weather compounds; no technical source claimed.

items.slot_note: Trap. The slash form gives only 'Schmidt'; in ChemE usage the technical candidate is almost always the 'Schmidt number' (Sc = momentum diffusivity / mass diffusivity), the mass-transfer analogue of the Prandtl number. It is decided by 'number' after the slot or by Sc/mass-transfer topic words. Ordinary 'Smith' is a surname — an author or person reference ('Smith and Van Ness', 'Smith et al.') — and is followed by 'and', 'et al.', or a verb, never by 'number' in the dimensionless sense.

candidates.label: Schmidt number
phrase_patterns: Schmidt number is the mass-transfer analogue of Prandtl number
candidates.notes: Source usage: 'the Schmidt number (Sc)... is a dimensionless number defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity (kinematic viscosity) and mass diffusivity'; 'physically relates the relative thickness of the hydrodynamic layer and mass-transfer boundary layer'; 'the heat transfer analog of the Schmidt number is the Prandtl number'.

candidates.label: Smith (ordinary surname)
candidates.notes: Structural: surname in author-pair and citation patterns (Smith is a standard ChemE thermodynamics textbook author name); a following 'number' rules this reading out.

items.slot_note: Alternatives share the head word Poisson and differ in the following noun: distribution or equation. candidates.label: Poisson distribution
